# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. Pairing covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. Rounds covers event stages. Boards and deals distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. Ties and scores address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

Reproducibility explains the existing technical tools. Competition research describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. Architecture, session module and React boundaries give the broader engineering context.

# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

Competition deals covers board identity. Competition ties covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores.

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.

# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in competition pairing, and the dimensions of the playing board are in competition boards.

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. Status bar explains the existing statistics, and React boundaries explains the surrounding composition.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. Mismatch interval and new game and restart cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. Focus policy and dialog policy describe the existing interactions.

# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in competition deals.

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterfinal | 4 | 16 | 8 |
| Semifinal | 6 | 36 | 18 |
| Final | 8 | 64 | 32 |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

Face catalogue, pair identity and card artwork cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See large board rendering, layout grid and zoom behaviour.

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. Board keyboard navigation covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in board code format; the fixed generation algorithm is in deck generation. Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. Snapshot format and snapshot selection notes explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outsid
... command output truncated for persistence ...
Rules. For the three alternatives themselves, see Selection state.

## What enters the core

The board supplies a position index to `useGame.activate`, which synchronizes active time before calling `activateSession`. A paused imported session blocks activation there; otherwise the session calls `activateCard` with the game and index.

The core reads neither a DOM node nor an input device. Pointer and keyboard activation share this position-based transition. Face identity comes from the value at that position, as explained in Pair identity.

## Guards before selection branching

The function returns the existing state for a noninteger index, a negative index, or an index at or beyond `deck.length`. It also returns that same state if `matched` already includes the position.

The integer check excludes fractional numbers, `NaN`, and infinities. Invalid activation does not start the game, add a move, or disturb a first selection. The matched-position check applies regardless of which selection alternative is current.

Returning the same object is observable by the session layer. It uses `game === session.game` to avoid treating an ignored operation as a turn result. A structurally identical fresh object would lose that inexpensive distinction.

There is no independent `isWon` guard at the beginning of `activateCard`. In a valid completed game every position is matched, so all in-range activation is already caught by the matched-position guard. This relies on the state invariants established by normal transitions and snapshot validation.

## First reveal

From closed selection, an eligible activation returns a new game with `started: true` and selection `{ kind: one, index }`. Deck, matched positions, moves, and elapsed time are preserved.

Repeated activation of that first position returns the existing state. A matched card is also ignored before this branch, leaving the first card available for another eligible position. No move is charged until that second position is revealed.

## Second reveal: shared work

In the one-card branch, the function reads the first position from `state.selection.index`. Once it has rejected a repeat of that same position, it calculates:

```ts
const moves = Math.min(MOVES_MAX, state.moves + 1);
```

`MOVES_MAX` is 999,999. This calculation is shared by both outcomes. A successful guess and an unsuccessful guess each complete a two-card attempt and cost one move, until the displayed counter reaches its cap.

The pair comparison is exactly:

```ts
state.deck[first] === state.deck[index]
```

It does not compare row numbers, card DOM identifiers, shape labels, or the order of activation. On a valid deck, each face has two occurrences, and the guards ensure the two eligible positions are distinct and unmatched.

The second reveal has no intermediate returned state where two equal cards remain merely selected. The comparison and resulting progress update are one pure call. A render sees the result of that call.

## Match path

For equal face values, the new game contains:

```ts
{
  ...state,
  moves,
  matched: [...state.matched, first, index],
  selection: { kind: SelectionKind.closed },
}
```

Appending the two indices records their positions as permanently revealed progress. Earlier matched positions retain their order in memory. Selection closes immediately, making another turn eligible without a mismatch wait.

On the example deal `np1-4-1`, positions 2 and 6 both contain face 0:

| Action | Selection | Moves | Matched |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Closed | 0 | Empty |
| Reveal 2 | One at 2 | 0 | Empty |
| Reveal 6 | Closed | 1 | 2, 6 |
| Activate 6 again | Unchanged | 1 | 2, 6 |
| Reveal 0 | One at 0 | 1 | 2, 6 |

The last action begins a new turn. The earlier successful pair stays visible because it is matched, not because the old selection remains open.

The same match path handles the final pair. Once the new `matched.length` equals the deck length, `isWon` reports completion. There is no special final-pair comparison or extra move. See Win conditions.

## Mismatch path

For different values, matched positions remain unchanged and selection becomes:

```ts
{
  kind: SelectionKind.mismatch,
  first,
  second: index,
  remainingMs: MISMATCH_MS,
}
```

`MISMATCH_MS` is 800. Both positions are face up while that selection is current. On the example deal, positions 0 and 1 contain faces 6 and 7, so revealing them from a fresh board gives one move and this mismatch.

Every subsequent activation returns the same state until active-time advancement closes the selection. A third-card activation is ignored rather than queued. Holding a position in a pending input list is not part of this implementation.

`advanceGame` subtracts the supplied positive active duration from `remainingMs`. At the exact boundary it replaces selection with closed. Closing does not add a move and does not record a pair. The next eligible activation begins another one-card selection.

For the example miss:

```text
reveal 0, reveal 1 -> mismatch, moves 1, remaining 800
advance 799       -> mismatch, moves 1, remaining 1
activate 2        -> unchanged
advance 1         -> closed, moves 1
activate 2        -> one at 2, moves 1
```

Elapsed time rules explains which browser intervals count as active, and Mismatch interval covers the precise closing boundary.

## Ordering time before activation

The browser synchronizes its clock before processing each activation. This can close an overdue mismatch immediately before the clicked position is evaluated. The result depends on the current logical time, rather than on whether a scheduled render callback happened to run first.

Suppose a mismatch started at monotonic time 362.25 milliseconds. At 1162.00 it still has 0.25 milliseconds remaining, so an activation at that moment is ignored. At 1162.25 or later, synchronization can close it first, after which a valid position begins the next turn.

This also explains an apparent state change during an otherwise ignored click. The click can cause clock synchronization to commit elapsed time or finish a mismatch even when the ensuing card activation is itself ignored. Move accounting remains tied to the core second-reveal rule. An ignored activation adds no move, while time continues to pass in an active game.

The replay path uses analogous ordering. It advances to each action's logical timestamp before activating the index. An interval ending exactly at that timestamp has therefore closed before the action. Equal-time actions retain their array order. The format is covered in Replay format.

## What the session adds

`activateSession` recognizes a first reveal because the returned selection is one. It updates the game without adding turn feedback. A completed two-card attempt follows a different path: it determines whether the result is a win, a mismatch, or an ordinary match, and updates the feedback text and announcement counter.

For a nonfinal successful match, feedback includes the number of pairs matched. The first uses singular wording and later results use plural wording. Mismatch feedback says the cards close after a short pause. Completion feedback includes final moves and formatted elapsed time.

A successful final activation also calls `rememberBest` and sets `celebration` to true. Those are session effects derived from a core transition. `activateCard` on its own produces no saved preference update, sound, message, or celebration flag.

A clock tick closing a mismatch goes through `tickSession`, which updates the game but does not create another turn announcement. The feedback can therefore still describe the most recent miss after its two cards have closed. It is the result of the last attempt, not a continuously rewritten description of selection.

## Replacement during an attempt

Game replacement discards the current selection and increments session generation, so an old clock callback cannot close a replacement game's new card. Restart recreates the same hidden code; New Game requests a fresh seed. New Game and Restart covers the shared replacement path.

## Practical evidence

`game.test.ts` checks known matching positions, repeated-first-card activation, invalid indices, blocking, and exact expiry. `move-cap.test.ts` checks continued turns at the saturated count. `session.test.ts` adds pause, feedback, and completion records.

For browser ordering, `tests/fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` checks a mismatch begun between whole milliseconds and an overdue click before a timer can run. A known code plus ordered indices and active-time steps is enough to distinguish comparison, counting, and timing defects.
# Elapsed time rules

This page explains active elapsed time, browser clock accounting, and display formatting in Neon Pairs.

`src/game/elapsed-time.ts` contains the formatter. Accumulation belongs to `advanceGame` in `game.ts`, and the browser decides which durations to supply through `session/use-session-clock.ts` and `session/browser-clock.ts`. Reading those three layers separately explains why rendering frequency does not define the measured duration.

## What counts as active

Elapsed time begins with the first valid reveal. Before that, `advanceGame` returns the existing state because `started` is false. Reading the controls or waiting at a fresh hidden board does not accrue game time.

Once started, time counts while the page is visible and the game is unfinished, unless an unfinished imported snapshot is awaiting Resume. It includes time spent looking at one revealed card, considering a choice between turns, and viewing a mismatch. It does not measure only the time when a pointer or keyboard is moving.

The browser running predicate combines four conditions:

```text
page visible
and session not paused
and game started
and game not won
```

The core knows only started and completion. Visibility and imported pause are browser-session concerns. Direct calls to `advanceGame` assume the caller has supplied an active duration.

There is no ordinary manual pause control during a played game. Resume is associated with loaded unfinished progress. Page visibility is based on `document.hidden`; the hook does not use window focus, pointer idleness, or the reproduction panel's open state as additional clock gates.

## Core accumulation

`advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` ignores a duration that is nonfinite or nonpositive. It also ignores it before start or after victory. For a valid active step:

```ts
const elapsedMs = Math.min(ELAPSED_MAX_MS, state.elapsedMs + milliseconds);
```

`ELAPSED_MAX_MS` is 359,999,999. The current implementation retains fractional milliseconds in memory, since monotonic browser observations can include fractions. It does not round each observation down before adding it.

The same call subtracts its delta from a pending mismatch. A large step can close the mismatch while adding the entire active duration to elapsed time. The 800-millisecond mismatch duration is not an upper bound on how much elapsed time that call can add.

Elapsed saturation does not end play. It also does not stop a mismatch countdown, because that countdown uses the original supplied delta. See Mismatch interval.

## Observing the browser clock

`browser-clock.ts` stores one observation in an `ActiveClock`: `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` initializes it. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes the difference from that observation, returning a positive finite difference only when active is true.

Every result includes a new clock observed at `now`, even when no duration was counted. Advancing the observation during inactivity is essential: the next active observation can then exclude the period spent waiting, hidden, or paused.

The browser hook reads `performance.now()` and uses recursive timeouts with a usual 40-millisecond interval. It measures the actual difference between readings. It does not add a fixed 40 merely because a callback ran.

For example, active readings at 0, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 3.7, and 10.9 accumulate the same duration, within floating-point precision, as a single active observation from 0 to 10.9. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks this property, along with fractional durations and inactive intervals.

That example concerns logical observation, not a guarantee of a 40-millisecond browser paint. A busy task can delay a callback. When it runs, the measured difference catches up the game to the observed active time.

## Start, actions, and completion boundaries

Before processing a card activation, `useGame.activate` synchronizes the clock. At the first reveal, the game is still unstarted during this synchronization, so earlier waiting is discarded and the observation point moves to the reveal's time. The activation then sets started to true.

Later activations synchronize while the game is active. This captures duration between rendered ticks and ensures an overdue mismatch can close before a new card is considered. At the final activation, synchronization captures time up to that action before the game becomes won.

After victory, the running predicate is false and `advanceGame` also refuses additional duration. The completion time is retained without waiting for the completion banner's visual effect to finish.

Export also synchronizes before encoding a snapshot. Thus exported progress can be ahead of the last ordinary rendered tick, while still corresponding to the current active clock. It does not rely on a status string that was formatted earlier.

## Visibility boundaries

The visibility listener synchronizes before changing its stored visibility flag. On the transition to hidden, it counts the active interval up to that observation. On the transition back to visible, it observes the intervening duration as inactive, then resumes scheduling.

Suppose the game starts, runs visibly for 300 milliseconds, then a miss runs visibly for another 200. Hiding for five seconds adds nothing. On return, another 600 active milliseconds finish the mismatch. The total elapsed duration is 1,100 milliseconds: 300 before the miss plus the miss's full 800 active milliseconds.

Counting wall-clock time between first reveal and completion would include the hidden five seconds and disagree with the game's definition. A reproduction of a clock issue needs the visibility changes as well as the overall wait.

The hook clears its scheduled timeout while inactive. The implementation also handles a synchronization request made during inactivity by updating the observation without counting that period.

## Imported pause and resets

An unfinished import retains its elapsed value and waits paused. Resume resets browser observation before clearing that pause, excluding the time spent inspecting the position. If started is false, the clock still waits for a valid first reveal. Completed imports remain stopped by victory.

Successful replacements also reset observation. New Game and Restart receive zero game time from `createGame`; snapshots retain their imported value. Invalid loads do neither reset nor replacement. New Game and Restart compares these operations.

## Display conversion

`formatElapsed` first floors milliseconds divided by 1,000. It then divides that whole-second count into minutes and a seconds remainder, padding the seconds to two digits:

```ts
const seconds = Math.floor(milliseconds / 1000);
const minutes = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
return `${minutes}:${String(seconds % 60).padStart(2, '0')}`;
```

| Stored milliseconds | Formatted value |
| ---: | --- |
| 0 | `0:00` |
| 999.9 | `0:00` |
| 1,000 | `0:01` |
| 59,999 | `0:59` |
| 60,000 | `1:00` |
| 3,600,000 | `60:00` |
| 359,999,999 | `5999:59` |

There is no separate hour field. Minutes continue past 59. `GameStatus` places the `Time:` label alongside this formatted value, and completion feedback uses the same formatter.

The formatter does not enforce the game's domain or cap its argument. It assumes a valid duration supplied by state. The cap is enforced by advancement and snapshot validation, so a direct unsupported call to the formatter is not an alternative game input path.

## Snapshot precision

`encodeSnapshot` floors elapsed milliseconds to a whole number. It rounds a pending mismatch remainder upward. These opposite rounding directions preserve the external constraints: elapsed is a whole nonnegative duration, and a still-pending mismatch has at least one millisecond remaining.

For an in-memory elapsed value of 11.75 and a mismatch remainder of 799.25, export writes elapsed 11 and remaining 800. Import restores those integer values. The live game keeps its fractions; export does not replace it with the rounded representation.

A round trip can therefore change submillisecond precision in the restored copy. That is expected at the format boundary. It does not justify rounding every browser tick, which would repeatedly discard fractions and make accumulated time depend on observation frequency.

The fractional browser test uses quarter milliseconds so its test values are exactly representable in binary. It checks both elapsed export and a final quarter-millisecond mismatch remainder exporting as 1.

## Replay uses explicit active time

Replay advances to each action's logical timestamp before activation, then to its end time. Waiting before the first valid reveal is ignored, and completion stops later advances. Hidden intervals and import pauses are omitted from this active timeline. Compare active durations when comparing replay and browser results; see Replay format.

## Source evidence

`elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the cap, exported capped progress, and rejection above the cap. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks fractional accumulation and inactive observations. `tests/clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` exports between scheduled ticks. `tests/idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` checks untouched hidden and paused intervals.

These are distinct checks: a formatter example verifies text, a core advance verifies arithmetic, and a browser journey verifies which intervals reach that arithmetic. A correct-looking status string alone cannot prove that a hidden period was excluded or that the final click was synchronized.
# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. Clock design discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. Mismatch interval covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. Elapsed time rules covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. Clock design follows those cases in detail, and Test policy explains the runners.

# ADR 054: Verify complete player journeys

This record explains why acceptance combines rule evidence with complete input, reproduction and delivery journeys.

## Context

A game can pass isolated assertions and still fail at the boundary between them. A new deal can look correct until an old mismatch callback closes a newly revealed card. A loaded snapshot can look correct until its Resume button disappears with focus still on it. Acceptance needs sequences that cross those boundaries.

The decision is to express acceptance as journeys tied to the existing product requirements. The acceptance specification explicitly says those examples add no rules beyond their defining documents. This record explains why journeys are useful evidence rather than another source of behavior requirements.

## The highest-value sequences

The play journey completes every supported size and checks move accounting, matches, misses and best records. The interruption journey starts or restarts during a mismatch and waits beyond the old interval. The keyboard journey enters the board, learns names, resolves turns, completes, leaves with Tab and starts again.

Reproduction journeys round-trip snapshots, reject malformed drafts and load unfinished progress. They attempt input while paused, Resume and check remaining active time. Delivery opens the freshly built HTML from disk with requests blocked, while persistence uses an HTTP origin. Each sequence joins behaviors that separate unit tests cannot establish by themselves.

## Example: a stale callback

A focused game test can prove that `createGame` returns zero moves and a closed selection. A session test can prove that a mismatched generation is ignored. The browser journey supplies the final connection: perform the mismatch, restart through the actual control, reveal a card and let earlier work become due. The newly revealed card must reflect the current game, not an old callback.

This is not redundant testing of one function at three levels. Each level answers a different question about the same product risk. Session module, ADR 013 and Regression catalogue explain the related mechanics.

## Example: accessibility as a sequence

A button can have a correct name in isolation while the whole game is difficult to traverse. The complete 4x4 keyboard journey checks controls, positional names, revealed faces, turn feedback, final summary and exit. Browser accessibility-tree evidence makes those observations reviewable.

A screen reader was not run during the recorded automated verification. Spoken confirmation belongs to user acceptance, as does the real-device long-press context menu. Keeping those boundaries explicit makes the automated evidence credible rather than overstating what browser automation can observe. Screen reader notes gives the player-facing account.

## Why not only end-to-end tests

Journey tests are expensive places to enumerate malformed JSON or every seed rejection edge. Focused tests isolate those cases faster and report more local failures. Acceptance selects meaningful combinations and user-visible consequences; it does not replace the core test suite.

Likewise, a screenshot at the end of a game cannot establish every transition that led there. Exact clock edges and parser invariants need structured assertions. The strategy uses complementary evidence rather than demanding that one test style prove everything.

## Build provenance and limitations

The browser command type checks and builds current source before journeys begin. Diagnostic entries are built separately, and the wrapper records runtime versions. A passing journey therefore has a concrete artifact and tool context. It still does not establish behavior on every browser, device or unsupported gesture.

Acceptance, ADR 017, ADR 018 and ADR 051 are the companion references. The decision keeps acceptance close to the player's actual task while preserving a clear boundary between requirements and examples that demonstrate them.

## The fresh-build browser command

The command sequence ties journeys to current source. A failed game or diagnostic build prevents the browser test process from running.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite --host 127.0.0.1",
    "typecheck": "tsc -p tsconfig.app.json && tsc -p tsconfig.node.json && tsc -p tsconfig.e2e.json",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "build": "npm run typecheck && vite build",
    "build:art": "vite build --config vite.art.config.ts && vite build --config vite.session.config.ts",
    "test:e2e": "npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 \"tests/*.e2e.test.ts\"",
    "replay": "node scripts/replay.ts",
    "format": "prettier --write .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check ."
  }
}
```
