| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. Pointer and touch explains the touch path to the last card; Board keyboard navigation explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. Zoom behaviour covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. Native controls guide explains that architectural advantage, while Contrast audit and Focus policy cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
# Native controls guide

This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface.

The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core.

## The current element choices

| Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes |
| `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal |
| `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids |
| `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code |
| `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder |
| `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
| `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout |
| `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values |

These choices describe the current DOM. Policies for other kinds of content are documented in Dialog policy and Tables policy, without implying that those elements already appear in Game.

## Buttons unify activation

Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.

The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.

Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.

A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. Disabled state guide explains that deliberate split.

## The select keeps its native interaction

Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior.

The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.

The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu.

A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. Control bar covers that data flow.

## Text editing remains text editing

Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency.

The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data.

BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea.

Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see Reproduction panel.

## A disclosure is already an interaction

The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.

The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation.

A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. Card artwork and Screen reader notes describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. Form layout guide and Target size policy cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. ADR 006 is the decision reference, while Architecture explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.
# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

Board keyboard navigation explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. Mismatch interval and Clock design describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. Reproduction panel describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. Error display guide traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in Rules:

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow Input and Controls. Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against Visuals. Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking Sound. Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check Reproducibility with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in Technology. Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against Architecture.

Back to Neon Pairs.
# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in Reproducibility.

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in Visuals.


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in Input. Return to Neon Pairs for the full specification.

# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in Name length policy and Duplicate names policy. This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.

A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.

## Drafts and accepted values

A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.

That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.

The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.

No name persistence shape exists in `session/storage.ts`. Its preferences concern size and best move counts. Those fields contain no name preference key, snapshot property or import format.

## Board codes follow a different path

The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path.

The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed.

Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See Reproduction panel.

Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant.

## Snapshot text remains structured data

Snapshot JSON has a native textarea length limit and a decoder byte limit. It can include whitespace for readability, and export deliberately produces multiple lines. Its structure is validated before the game is replaced.

Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.

The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.

Import safety policy and Error display guide explain the current parser and feedback boundaries. Keeping those links close to the input descriptions is more useful than inventing one universal cleanup function for every field on the page.

## Unicode review considerations

Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot.

The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.

Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. Typography provides the visual context.

The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.

## Implementation evidence to look for

There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.

Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.

The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.
# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in Text entry policy. Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The Duplicate names policy addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.
# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only rep…8028 tokens truncated…le and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. Card artwork and Screen reader notes describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. Form layout guide and Target size policy cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. ADR 006 is the decision reference, while Architecture explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.
# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

Board keyboard navigation explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. Mismatch interval and Clock design describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. Reproduction panel describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. Error display guide traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in Rules:

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow Input and Controls. Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against Visuals. Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking Sound. Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check Reproducibility with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in Technology. Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against Architecture.

Back to Neon Pairs.
# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in Reproducibility.

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in Visuals.


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in Input. Return to Neon Pairs for the full specification.
