# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes ADR 011. The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. Preferences store and Storage failure policy describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

## The current preferences key and value shape

These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```
# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in Board code format.

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. Snapshot format gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. Replay format covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See Reproduction panel and Focus policy for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. Import safety describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.
# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual fo
... command output truncated for persistence ...
ook for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. Source audit notes describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. CSS organization traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, Code review guide starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, Architecture remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. Session module explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. Clock design details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.
# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. Native controls guide explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. Control bar documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. Error display guide follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. Text entry policy, Name length policy and Duplicate names policy own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order.
# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. Announcements policy describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## Who decides that a load failed

BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement.

Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself.

`SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler.

This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first.

## What a failure preserves

A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean.

The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared.

Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference.

The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. Game state model and Session module explain those boundaries.

## Focus depends on how submission began

A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing.

On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump.

Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically.

These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. Focus policy covers the complete set of current focus transfers.

## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

`loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel.

After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values.

Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction.

Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play.

This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state.

## Format validity is more than native limits

Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair.

Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error.

The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. Import safety policy and Snapshot format are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft.

A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class.

## Existing visual and semantic treatment

The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run.

The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. Form layout guide explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure.

Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in Name length policy and Duplicate names policy. The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component.

## Evidence for preservation and retry

`tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause.

`tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys.

A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning.
