# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.
# ADR 023: Present rankings as ordered lists

This historical record explains the retired ordered-list presentation for rankings and results.

Status: Superseded by Tables policy

## Original context

The early results sketch emphasized a phone-sized page. A sequence of entries could be stacked vertically, with the name and result together and little need for horizontal movement. At that point, the team chose ordered lists for rankings and results because they read well on phones.

This was a presentation decision in the original design discussion; the current game has no ranking screen. The current playable implementation shows its own move count, pair progress, time and per-size best.

## Decision as made

Each entry would have been one list row, with ordering carrying the ranking meaning. Supporting text could sit under the primary name without creating a wide grid. The list's native numbering appeared to provide a useful relationship between visual position and reading order.

The design favored following one entry from top to bottom over scanning one metric down a column. That was a reasonable priority while the imagined result was a short linear reading task. It also made the narrow-screen prototype straightforward to build using familiar block layout.

## Reasons that supported the choice

An ordered list can express a sequence without an additional position field in every visible row. It adapts naturally to wrapping text, and native list semantics are familiar to accessibility tools. With few fields, a list gives each entry enough vertical space without forcing a compact row height.

The team also wanted to avoid a horizontal scrolling area outside the game board. A stacked entry appeared to solve that on small screens and kept the imagined results section visually close to ordinary prose. The old decision therefore came from a concrete reading concern, not from treating a list as a universally better data structure.

## Alternatives discussed

A tabular layout was more structured and better suited to comparisons across repeated fields. In the earliest sketch, that benefit seemed less urgent than fitting an entire entry into a phone width. Cards for individual results were another option, but they would have added visual framing while leaving the same question of how to compare one field across entries.

Plain paragraphs were rejected as too weak a representation of order. A manually typed rank inside every paragraph would have reproduced part of an ordered list without its structural meaning. The initial list choice was therefore internally coherent for the information the sketch expected to emphasize.

## Why this is historical

The weakness of a stacked list becomes apparent when readers want to compare the same metric across several entries. Repeated labels take space, and values no longer align in a way that supports scanning. The original rationale optimized the reading of an individual result and gave less weight to cross-entry relationships.

Tables policy is the replacement decision. The relevant historical lesson is that narrow-screen layout alone was too small a basis for choosing a representation of comparative data. The information's relationships also matter.

## Connection to the current code

`GameStatus.tsx` uses a definition list for the current game's labeled statistics and a paragraph for completion. That is a different information shape from a ranked collection of participants. It should not be interpreted as an implementation of this old ordered-list decision or as evidence against the replacement page.

Status bar, Tables policy and Interface review checklist are useful companions when reviewing actual screens. The superseding link at the top is the authority boundary: this historical rationale can explain a prototype, but it does not direct a new results presentation.
# ADR 053: Keep specifications near the implementation

This record explains repository documentation as a reviewable companion to code, tests and reproducible examples.

## Decision

Keep the product specification with the project so a behavior change can be understood alongside its implementation and evidence. The product specification belongs in `docs/` alongside the source.

Repository documentation was chosen because the game has precise rules that are not obvious from a screenshot. The mismatch interval is active time, Restart repeats a code, unfinished imports pause, and a closed card must not expose identity. These details deserve readable explanations rather than only test assertions or comments scattered through components.

## Different documents do different work

The rules page defines game behavior. Technology describes compiler settings, package pins, commands and delivery. Architecture explains pure functions and browser adapters. Acceptance provides journeys that exercise those definitions. Decision records explain why a choice was made and preserve retired reasoning when it is superseded.

That separation lets an engineer find the right level of answer. A parser field list belongs in the format description; the reason for choosing JSON belongs in ADR 010. A browser test can show a focus edge passing; ADR 024 explains why focus is remembered independently of selection.

## Why version control helps

A documentation change can be reviewed in the same context as a changed rule or component. An exact board code or replay example can remain attached to the version of the behavior it describes. Superseded records can link to their replacements without erasing the rationale that shaped older code or prototypes.

An external wiki might be convenient to edit, but it can drift from the source revision a reader has checked out. Generated API reference would identify function signatures without explaining the session boundaries or product intent. Comments alone would make cross-cutting journeys difficult to assemble. Repository prose complements those mechanisms rather than replacing all of them.

## Code remains evidence

A page that says a behavior exists is weaker than the source and tests when they disagree. The current game can be inspected through `Game.tsx`, the session adapter and pure core. Documentation names those real boundaries so a reader can verify an account instead of relying on a vague architectural diagram.

The same discipline applies to scope choices. The game has no locale framework or dedicated print stylesheet. Decision records explain those choices and distinguish historical reasoning from current implementation.

## Examples and links

The documentation set links related pages by filename. A reader can move from board-code syntax to seeded generation, from snapshot validation to import pause, or from large-board layout to focus scrolling. Links are most useful when they lead to a different level of explanation rather than repeat the same paragraph on several pages.

Examples use documented codes and public formats rather than hidden debugging endpoints. That keeps the explanation useful for a developer, a coding agent or a person investigating a report. The same examples can inform focused tests and browser fixtures, though expected test values still need independent justification.

## Costs

Prose needs maintenance. Moving behavior can leave stale source paths, and copying a rule into many pages can create conflicting versions. The repository location makes that drift reviewable; it does not prevent it automatically. Documentation style, ADR 054 and Code review guide explain the supporting habits without requiring a separate documentation service.

The outcome is a project whose behavior, implementation and reasons can be read together.
# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. Module layout policy explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the UI, and imports `game.css`. Its output is a single main element containing the heading, instructions, deal controls, statistics, turn feedback, board and reproduction controls.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. CSS organization records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
| `deck.ts` | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts` | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union |
| `game.ts` | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement |
| `elapsed-time.ts` | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds |
| `saved-format.ts` | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection |
| `snapshot.ts` | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation |
| `replay.ts` | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-session-clock.ts` supplies observations, maintains visibility, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, rep…27 tokens truncated….

## Why a flag system was unnecessary

Feature flags are useful when a deployed service needs staged rollout or different cohorts. Neon Pairs is distributed as a complete offline artifact. A person retains the file they have, and the project can build another revision. There is no runtime service coordinating a rollout across players.

A flag around a changed generator would be especially dangerous if the public code prefix stayed the same. The format version already provides the relevant boundary for generation changes. A flag around an import parser could likewise make the same JSON load on one copy and fail on another without an explicit format distinction. Format versioning guide explains the existing mechanism.

## Branches that are not feature flags

The application naturally branches on state. A mismatch blocks activation; an imported game may be paused; a completed board shows a banner; reduced-motion preference changes effects. These branches express documented session and browser behavior. They are not alternate product experiments controlled by a rollout service.

Tests also have configuration switches. `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` asks the browser wrapper to verify exact runtime versions. `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` can select a browser executable. Those values are read in test infrastructure, not by the shipped game to change matching or formats. The source-conventions test limits environment reads to the runners that need them.

## Diagnostic builds are separate

The artwork sheet and session harness are separate entries with separate Vite configurations. They do not use a production flag to reveal hidden test controls inside the game. This keeps the distributed entry focused on documented controls and reduces the risk of shipping a diagnostic branch accidentally.

A hash that secretly switches the face sheet into a session harness would blur that boundary. The art test explicitly checks that such a hash does not change the page's role. ADR 051 explains the evidence structure.

## Alternatives and costs

Keeping an old implementation behind a toggle can make rollback look convenient, but both branches then need coherent tests and format interpretation. A local development boolean is also easy to forget when building the final artifact. For this small game, normal source history supplies the record of retired approaches without keeping them executable in every copy.

The cost is that the game does not support selectively enabling unfinished features for different players. That capability is outside the current product and would require its own design if ever justified.

ADR 016, ADR 027, Source audit notes and ADR 052 explain the neighboring choices. The useful outcome is a reportable behavior path whose important variations are already named in game state, browser preferences and versioned data.

## Environment reads belong to runners

The source convention compares environment-read locations with the command and test runner needs. These are tooling controls, not product rollout flags.

```ts
test('source reads only the environment its command and test runners need', async () => {
  const reads = (await typescriptFiles()).flatMap((file) =>
    [...file.text.matchAll(ENVIRONMENT)].map((match) => `${file.path}:${match[1] ?? match[2]}`),
  );
  const runners = [
    'scripts/replay-cli.ts:INIT_CWD',
    'scripts/replay.test.ts:npm_execpath',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:EXECUTABLE_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:NAMED_COMBINATION_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:NPM_AGENT_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:TEMP',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:TMP',
  ];
  assert.deepEqual([...new Set(reads.map((read) => read.replaceAll('\\', '/')))].sort(), runners);
});
```
# ADR 043: Use the same action across input methods

This record explains keyboard parity for revealing cards while keeping navigation separate from play.

## Decision

A primary click, completed tap, Enter and Space reach the same card activation. Keyboard movement is a separate operation that changes focus without revealing a face. The choice gives different input methods the same game rules while preserving the browser's familiar controls.

The implementation uses native card buttons with one click handler calling the controller. It does not maintain a second keyboard-only move counter or a separate touch selection. Eligibility belongs to `activateCard`, which handles repeated first-card activation, matched cards and pending mismatches consistently for all callers.

## What parity means here

Parity does not mean every physical gesture has an identical event sequence. A tap can become a pan, a context-menu gesture has its own browser behavior, and Enter and Space follow native button activation timing. The shared result is the game action after a valid activation, not a demand to intercept every low-level event.

Hover and pointer cancellation leave game state unchanged. Right-click and long-press retain the context menu. Plain arrow keys move focus spatially; modifier combinations and other keys remain with the browser. This bounded key handling avoids turning the board into a page-wide keyboard interceptor. Input is the interaction definition.

## Focus is not selection

A focused card can be closed, revealed or matched. Moving the outline does not change the turn. During a mismatch, the player can still navigate although a reveal attempt is ignored. Matched cards stay focusable so known information remains inspectable.

The remembered tab stop makes entering a large board manageable, and native Tab leaves it. New deals reset that memory without moving focus away from the action button. Resume moves focus before removing its own button because it is a different lifecycle case. ADR 024 and Focus policy cover those details.

## Alternatives

Separate handlers that implement matching directly for each input method would make drift likely. One might count a repeated selection differently, or a touch path might reveal before a scroll gesture completed. Handling pointer down for fast visual response would also change the meaning of cancellation and context menus.

A keyboard-only “select” mode was unnecessary because native buttons already provide activation and the rules already describe a first and second reveal. A canvas board could simulate parity but would need custom focus and semantics before it reached the same starting point as DOM controls.

## Evidence

Focused rule tests prove that an activation has one meaning. Browser input tests then prove that the supported controls reach that action and that focus movement does not. The complete accessibility journey starts with controls, enters a 4x4 board, exposes positions and face names, completes the board, leaves with Tab and starts again.

The tree record is automated evidence about available names and states. Spoken output with a screen reader remains acceptance work. Touch scrolling is tested in browser automation, while real-device long-press remains an explicit manual observation. These limits keep the parity claim tied to the documented actions rather than every conceivable gesture.

Pointer and touch, Board keyboard navigation, ADR 022 and ADR 047 provide the related interaction rationale. The central outcome is one game transition path, surrounded by input-specific browser behavior rather than duplicated game rules.

## The card event boundary

Focus and navigation callbacks remain distinct from the click callback. The latter calls the shared activation before its completed-click scroll adjustment.

```tsx
return (
    <button
      type="button"
      className={`card ${state}`}
      aria-label={label}
      aria-disabled={matched}
      tabIndex={tabIndex}
      onFocus={(event) => focus(index, event.currentTarget)}
      onKeyDown={(event) => navigate(event, index)}
      onClick={(event) => {
        activate(index);
        clicked(event.currentTarget);
      }}
    >
      {face === null ? <span className="card-back" aria-hidden="true" /> : <Face face={face} />}
      {matched && (
        <svg className="matched-mark" viewBox="0 0 12 12" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
          <path d="m2 6 3 3 5-6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" />
        </svg>
      )}
    </button>
  );
});
```
# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in Rules.

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in Reproducibility. A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in Input.

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in Neon Pairs.
# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in competition ties. Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

Preferences store and best score records explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. Persistence overview and React boundaries cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
# ADR 040: Keep the delivered game compact

This record explains the compact-artifact aim and its architectural tradeoffs.

## Context

The one-file distribution should be easy to retain and pass along. Generated artwork, a system font and a narrow runtime help keep that artifact manageable. The team wanted compact delivery, with no maximum HTML byte count specified.

The size rules that are explicit concern authored TypeScript files: an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 lines per file. Those limits are about reviewable behavior modules, not compressed distribution size. Conflating the two would make a smaller source file look like proof of a smaller bundle when it might simply add another import.

## What actually affects the artifact

React and React DOM are bundled runtime dependencies. Vite and its plugins transform the source during the build. The face renderer describes shapes with a small set of SVG primitives rather than embedding 128 raster images. The system font avoids a downloaded or inlined font asset. There is no audio collection to carry with the file.

A single inline file also has no chunk-preload purpose. The main configuration disables the helper and the output test checks its absence. That removes irrelevant runtime machinery, though the reason is the offline contract rather than a claim about a particular number of saved bytes. ADR 003 explains delivery.

## Source structure is a separate optimization

Small modules make changes easier to review and focused tests easier to locate. They do not require collapsing every abstraction to reduce import statements. The build combines source modules into the final artifact, so a clear behavior boundary can remain in source without becoming another file the player must copy.

The current source audit measures authored TypeScript line counts and checks several source conventions. It does not report a universal bundle-size threshold. A developer reading this record can distinguish an enforced source constraint from a qualitative artifact aim. Source audit notes and ADR 057 explain that evidence.

## Alternatives

Removing React could reduce runtime code, but would exchange framework bytes for custom rendering and lifecycle work. Replacing generated SVG with raster sprites might compress differently, but would create asset maintenance and minimum-size review costs. Splitting the output into cached files could benefit a repeatedly visited hosted site while weakening the copy-one-file distribution path.

The project accepted the runtime framework in exchange for clear state-driven rendering. It rejected unnecessary remote assets and diagnostic code in the shipped entry. These are explicit architectural trades, not an assertion that the current bundle is the smallest possible implementation of a memory game.

## Measurement and interpretation

A meaningful artifact comparison uses the same build tools and compares the produced `dist/index.html`. Source character count, compressed transfer size and disk size answer different questions.

Diagnostic face-sheet and session outputs are separate builds. Their size should not be confused with the game artifact, just as test-result screenshots should not be counted as shipped resources. ADR 051 explains that separation.

The practical aim is to keep additions proportionate to a bounded offline game while preserving readable code and correct input. Dependency policy, Build pipeline and ADR 029 provide the neighboring context. The existing requirements and tests define what must pass today.

## The authored-source size check

The implemented size check counts lines in authored TypeScript. It should not be reported as a measurement of the final HTML bundle.

```ts
test('authored TypeScript stays small, uses static ESM and rejects unsafe type escapes', async () => {
  const files = (await Promise.all(['src', 'scripts', 'tests', 'art'].map(sourceFiles))).flat();
  for (const file of files.filter((file) => /\.tsx?$/.test(file.path))) {
    assert.ok(file.text.trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/).length <= 200, file.path);
    assert.doesNotMatch(file.text, /@ts-(?:ignore|nocheck|expect-error)/);
    assert.doesNotMatch(
      file.text,
      /\bany\b|\bas\s+(?:[A-Z{]|unknown\b|number\b|string\b)|\bimport\s*\(|\brequire\s*\(/,
    );
  }
});
```

# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
# ADR 040: Keep the delivered game compact

This record explains the compact-artifact aim and its architectural tradeoffs.

## Context

The one-file distribution should be easy to retain and pass along. Generated artwork, a system font and a narrow runtime help keep that artifact manageable. The team wanted compact delivery, with no maximum HTML byte count specified.

The size rules that are explicit concern authored TypeScript files: an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 lines per file. Those limits are about reviewable behavior modules, not compressed distribution size. Conflating the two would make a smaller source file look like proof of a smaller bundle when it might simply add another import.

## What actually affects the artifact

React and React DOM are bundled runtime dependencies. Vite and its plugins transform the source during the build. The face renderer describes shapes with a small set of SVG primitives rather than embedding 128 raster images. The system font avoids a downloaded or inlined font asset. There is no audio collection to carry with the file.

A single inline file also has no chunk-preload purpose. The main configuration disables the helper and the output test checks its absence. That removes irrelevant runtime machinery, though the reason is the offline contract rather than a claim about a particular number of saved bytes. ADR 003 explains delivery.

## Source structure is a separate optimization

Small modules make changes easier to review and focused tests easier to locate. They do not require collapsing every abstraction to reduce import statements. The build combines source modules into the final artifact, so a clear behavior boundary can remain in source without becoming another file the player must copy.

The current source audit measures authored TypeScript line counts and checks several source conventions. It does not report a universal bundle-size threshold. A developer reading this record can distinguish an enforced source constraint from a qualitative artifact aim. Source audit notes and ADR 057 explain that evidence.

## Alternatives

Removing React could reduce runtime code, but would exchange framework bytes for custom rendering and lifecycle work. Replacing generated SVG with raster sprites might compress differently, but would create asset maintenance and minimum-size review costs. Splitting the output into cached files could benefit a repeatedly visited hosted site while weakening the copy-one-file distribution path.

The project accepted the runtime framework in exchange for clear state-driven rendering. It rejected unnecessary remote assets and diagnostic code in the shipped entry. These are explicit architectural trades, not an assertion that the current bundle is the smallest possible implementation of a memory game.

## Measurement and interpretation

A meaningful artifact comparison uses the same build tools and compares the produced `dist/index.html`. Source character count, compressed transfer size and disk size answer different questions.

Diagnostic face-sheet and session outputs are separate builds. Their size should not be confused with the game artifact, just as test-result screenshots should not be counted as shipped resources. ADR 051 explains that separation.

The practical aim is to keep additions proportionate to a bounded offline game while preserving readable code and correct input. Dependency policy, Build pipeline and ADR 029 provide the neighboring context. The existing requirements and tests define what must pass today.

## The authored-source size check

The implemented size check counts lines in authored TypeScript. It should not be reported as a measurement of the final HTML bundle.

```ts
test('authored TypeScript stays small, uses static ESM and rejects unsafe type escapes', async () => {
  const files = (await Promise.all(['src', 'scripts', 'tests', 'art'].map(sourceFiles))).flat();
  for (const file of files.filter((file) => /\.tsx?$/.test(file.path))) {
    assert.ok(file.text.trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/).length <= 200, file.path);
    assert.doesNotMatch(file.text, /@ts-(?:ignore|nocheck|expect-error)/);
    assert.doesNotMatch(
      file.text,
      /\bany\b|\bas\s+(?:[A-Z{]|unknown\b|number\b|string\b)|\bimport\s*\(|\brequire\s*\(/,
    );
  }
});
```

# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see Reproduction panel.

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in Board keyboard navigation.

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. Pointer and touch explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See Preferences store for the exact validation and React effect. Best score records covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see Snapshot format and Reproduction panel.

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. Offline delivery describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. Private browsing notes and Storage quota notes separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.
