# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in Persistence envelope. Parsing and validation failures are covered in Corrupt data policy, because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. Best score records explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. Storage quota notes discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See Preferences store for the exact validation and React effect. Best score records covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see Snapshot format and Reproduction panel.

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See Format versioning guide and Data exchange policy when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

Preferences store documents the complete aggregate reader. Persistence overview explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks

`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.

The object checks are structural, not class checks. `isJsonObject` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` accepts an object if it is non-null and not an array. That helper alone says nothing about which fields are present. The reader supplies the field-specific checks after narrowing the parsed value.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.
## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. Import safety describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

docs/source-layout.md:11:`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

docs/react-boundaries.md:28:| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
docs/release-notes-1-4.md:23:Resume has a focus consequence because its button disappears. docs/architecture.md:38:- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes solo play or Tournament mode. docs/adr-024-roving-focus.md:21:`Game.tsx` keys the board with the session generation. A successful new deal, Restart or load replaces the board's focus memory and starts again at the first position. docs/time-policy.md:75:Restarting the same board still changes the generation. docs/session-module.md:43:Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.
docs/session-module.md:57:The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.
docs/competition-research.md:21:This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. docs/documentation-style.md:27:Source references are most useful when they explain responsibility. `src/game/game.ts` owns card transitions and logical time. `src/game/session/session.ts` wraps them with feedback and preferences. `src/game/session/use-game.ts` connects loading, exporting and React state. `src/game/Game.tsx` composes the screen. A page about a turn can begin in the core and follow only the layers relevant to its question.
docs/focus-policy.md:9:`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. docs/focus-policy.md:45:In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. docs/card-artwork.md:14:A board replacement changes the `Board` key through `session.generation` in `Game.tsx`. The new board consequently starts a fresh local focus memory. That is independent of whether some numeric positions happen to have the same face as the earlier deal. See New game and restart for the session behavior.
docs/accessibility-audit.md:59:The session tracks an announcement number, and `Game.tsx` keys the feedback span with that event value. Identical wording can therefore represent successive events. The announcement tests install a MutationObserver and compare observed result changes with the expected sequence, including repeated invalid loads and repeated misses.
docs/accessibility-audit.md:67:New Game, Restart, load and export actions preserve focus on their initiating control. Resume is different because it removes itself: `Game.tsx` calls the board's remembered-focus method before clearing pause. The control-contract and snapshot browser cases inspect that ordering.
docs/reproduction-panel.md:9:`Game.tsx` renders Reproduction after the Board. Its native `details` element has class `reproduction` and no `open` attribute, so it starts collapsed. The summary reads `Reproduce a game`, taken from `ReproductionControl.summary` in `control-labels.ts`. Opening and closing the disclosure is browser behavior; the component has no separate expanded-state variable.
docs/reproduction-panel.md:60:`Game.tsx` wraps resume in a function that first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. The order gives focus a durable target before the Resume button disappears. The controller resets its clock adapter, clears `paused`, `feedback` and `loadNotice`, and leaves the loaded game state in place. If a pending mismatch had 300ms left when saved, it continues for that remaining active interval after Resume.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:9:`src/game/game.ts` owns selection and matching. `src/game/session/session.ts` derives turn feedback after an accepted activation. `src/game/Game.tsx` brings the board, status and feedback together. There is no audio step between a successful state change and its presentation.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:86:`Game.tsx` renders `session.feedback` inside a paragraph with `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`. The sentence is ordinary visible text as well as accessible status content. It is not a transcript of audio generated by the application.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:110:New Game and Restart replace the current session game through `replaceGame`. That clears the previous feedback and load notice, removes the celebration flag and increments the generation. The board is keyed by that generation in `Game.tsx`, which resets its remembered focus position with the replacement. The player sees a closed board and cleared counters rather than a reset sound.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:118:The Resume handler in `Game.tsx` focuses the board's remembered card and then calls the controller's resume action. That action clears feedback and load notice while leaving the imported game intact. If the imported selection was a mismatch, its remaining active interval can now continue. Resume does not manufacture a new pair result for the saved selection.
docs/research-screen-reader-sessions.md:45:The keyed feedback span in `Game.tsx` is important here because equal strings do not necessarily cause a new text mutation. A second identical miss is still another attempt. The current browser announcement tests observe result changes around these cases; they do not listen to a screen reader speaking them.
docs/audio-research-notes.md:75:The game paths described above change state and DOM without an audio service, media element or playback call. `Game.tsx` composes visual and semantic output directly. The following tests cover these paths.
docs/adr-044-no-routing.md:9:The decision is to keep the application as one page with direct component composition and no router. `Game.tsx` renders controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction in a single `main`. The architecture specification explicitly avoids a routing framework for this scope.
docs/meeting-notes-accessibility.md:27:The group then followed a miss, another identical miss, a match, and the final pair. This sequence matters because repeated equal text can be one event in a renderer even when it represents two turns to a person. Current `Session.announcement` advances for each published result, and the keyed span in `Game.tsx` makes the event visible to the DOM.
docs/meeting-notes-accessibility.md:41:Resume raised a different focus question. An unfinished imported board is paused; selecting Resume removes that button. Current `Game.tsx` focuses the board's remembered card before clearing the pause. New Game, Restart, loading, and export controls remain focused because their buttons remain present. These are different lifecycle cases, even though all may leave the board looking newly ready to play.
docs/adr-053-docs-in-repo.md:25:A page that says a behavior exists is weaker than the source and tests when they disagree. The current game can be inspected through `Game.tsx`, the session adapter and pure core. Documentation names those real boundaries so a reader can verify an account instead of relying on a vague architectural diagram.
docs/adr-001-react.md:13:React represents the current session; it does not define what a match means. `src/game/game.ts` implements `activateCard` and `advanceGame` without React. `useGame` adapts those operations to browser state, and `Game.tsx` composes `Controls`, `GameStatus`, `Board` and `Reproduction`. This boundary lets replay call the same rules without constructing a document or mounting a component.
docs/adr-001-react.md:40:import { Game } from './game/Game.tsx';
docs/competition-boards.md:19:The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.
docs/competition-overview.md:13:The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.
docs/competition-overview.md:41:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.
docs/competition-research.md:63:This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.
docs/competition-pairing.md:52:The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores.
docs/competition-pairing.md:58:The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.
docs/competition-scores.md:46:There is no competition argument or mode check in either solo function. The boundary is enforced at the controller composition: tournament games are separate from the `Session` whose preferences those functions update.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:33:The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.
docs/competition-rounds.md:13:The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.
docs/competition-rounds.md:17:A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.
docs/competition-rounds.md:25:`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.
docs/persistence-overview.md:17:The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.
docs/competition-ties.md:75:A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.
docs/retention-policy.md:41:For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:26:A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

Reading only the introduction is enough to begin.
docs/module-layout-policy.md:17:The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.
docs/module-layout-policy.md:53:Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.
docs/source-layout.md:11:`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.
docs/source-layout.md:17:`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the solo UI, and switches to the Tournament screen while keeping the solo session mounted and its clock inactive. Its output is a single main element containing the heading and either the solo controls, statistics, board and reproduction tools or tournament setup, bracket, JSON tools and history.
docs/new-game-and-restart.md:…1413 tokens truncated…uction after the Board. Its native `details` element has class `reproduction` and no `open` attribute, so it starts collapsed. The summary reads `Reproduce a game`, taken from `ReproductionControl.summary` in `control-labels.ts`. Opening and closing the disclosure is browser behavior; the component has no separate expanded-state variable.
docs/reproduction-panel.md:60:`Game.tsx` wraps resume in a function that first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. The order gives focus a durable target before the Resume button disappears. The controller resets its clock adapter, clears `paused`, `feedback` and `loadNotice`, and leaves the loaded game state in place. If a pending mismatch had 300ms left when saved, it continues for that remaining active interval after Resume.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:9:`src/game/game.ts` owns selection and matching. `src/game/session/session.ts` derives turn feedback after an accepted activation. `src/game/Game.tsx` brings the board, status and feedback together. There is no audio step between a successful state change and its presentation.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:86:`Game.tsx` renders `session.feedback` inside a paragraph with `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`. The sentence is ordinary visible text as well as accessible status content. It is not a transcript of audio generated by the application.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:110:New Game and Restart replace the current session game through `replaceGame`. That clears the previous feedback and load notice, removes the celebration flag and increments the generation. The board is keyed by that generation in `Game.tsx`, which resets its remembered focus position with the replacement. The player sees a closed board and cleared counters rather than a reset sound.
docs/feedback-without-audio.md:118:The Resume handler in `Game.tsx` focuses the board's remembered card and then calls the controller's resume action. That action clears feedback and load notice while leaving the imported game intact. If the imported selection was a mismatch, its remaining active interval can now continue. Resume does not manufacture a new pair result for the saved selection.
docs/research-screen-reader-sessions.md:45:The keyed feedback span in `Game.tsx` is important here because equal strings do not necessarily cause a new text mutation. A second identical miss is still another attempt. The current browser announcement tests observe result changes around these cases; they do not listen to a screen reader speaking them.
docs/audio-research-notes.md:75:The game paths described above change state and DOM without an audio service, media element or playback call. `Game.tsx` composes visual and semantic output directly. The following tests cover these paths.
docs/adr-044-no-routing.md:9:The decision is to keep the application as one page with direct component composition and no router. `Game.tsx` renders controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction in a single `main`. The architecture specification explicitly avoids a routing framework for this scope.
docs/meeting-notes-accessibility.md:27:The group then followed a miss, another identical miss, a match, and the final pair. This sequence matters because repeated equal text can be one event in a renderer even when it represents two turns to a person. Current `Session.announcement` advances for each published result, and the keyed span in `Game.tsx` makes the event visible to the DOM.
docs/meeting-notes-accessibility.md:41:Resume raised a different focus question. An unfinished imported board is paused; selecting Resume removes that button. Current `Game.tsx` focuses the board's remembered card before clearing the pause. New Game, Restart, loading, and export controls remain focused because their buttons remain present. These are different lifecycle cases, even though all may leave the board looking newly ready to play.
docs/adr-053-docs-in-repo.md:25:A page that says a behavior exists is weaker than the source and tests when they disagree. The current game can be inspected through `Game.tsx`, the session adapter and pure core. Documentation names those real boundaries so a reader can verify an account instead of relying on a vague architectural diagram.
docs/adr-001-react.md:13:React represents the current session; it does not define what a match means. `src/game/game.ts` implements `activateCard` and `advanceGame` without React. `useGame` adapts those operations to browser state, and `Game.tsx` composes `Controls`, `GameStatus`, `Board` and `Reproduction`. This boundary lets replay call the same rules without constructing a document or mounting a component.
docs/adr-001-react.md:40:import { Game } from './game/Game.tsx';
docs/competition-boards.md:19:The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.
docs/competition-overview.md:13:The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.
docs/competition-overview.md:41:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.
docs/competition-research.md:63:This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.
docs/competition-pairing.md:52:The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores.
docs/competition-pairing.md:58:The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.
docs/competition-scores.md:46:There is no competition argument or mode check in either solo function. The boundary is enforced at the controller composition: tournament games are separate from the `Session` whose preferences those functions update.
docs/adr-058-storage-namespace.md:33:The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.
docs/competition-rounds.md:13:The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.
docs/competition-rounds.md:17:A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.
docs/competition-rounds.md:25:`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.
docs/persistence-overview.md:17:The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.
docs/competition-ties.md:75:A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.
docs/retention-policy.md:41:For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:26:A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

item.aggregated_output: # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet `tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause. Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result. New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load. Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains. ## Load outcomes share the publication path The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again. For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch. Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel. Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication. ## Completion and persistent reading GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time. The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game. A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did. ## Automated evidence `session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser. `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure. The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role. The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance. ## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text. For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page. # Tables policy This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure. There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented. ## Policy for result data When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning. This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things. No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format. ## Why the statistics are a definition list GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read. The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure. The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen. Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns. ## Why the card board is not a table Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model. The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle. There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts. ## What the caption contributes An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures. The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy. A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret. ## Column relationships and reading order The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure. A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface. Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details. ## Narrow layouts and long values The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow. There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence. Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface. The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context. # Feedback without audio This page explains how Neon Pairs makes actions, turn results and completion understandable while the game stays silent. The current contract is Sound, specification version 2.2. Silence covers revealing a card, finding a pair, missing a pair, resetting a deal and finishing the board. The application has no audio files, playback calls or sound control. This is a complete mode of play rather than a muted version waiting for someone to enable its feedback. ## Follow the change from state to display `src/game/game.ts` owns selection and matching. `src/game/session/session.ts` derives turn feedback after an accepted activation. `src/game/Game.tsx` brings the board, status and feedback together. There is no audio step between a successful state change and its presentation. | Player action or event | Card and status response | Result feedback | | --- | --- | --- | | Reveal the first eligible card | Its face replaces the back; the clock starts if this is the first reveal | The existing result text is unchanged | | Activate that same first card again | Selection and moves are unchanged | No new turn result | | Reveal a matching second card | Both faces remain visible with match marks; moves and pairs update | A pair-found sentence | | Reveal a nonmatching second card | Both faces remain visible for the mismatch interval; moves update | A no-match sentence | | Mismatch time expires | Both selected faces return to their common backs | The previous result remains; closing adds no result | | Activate an already matched card | The matched card stays as it is | No new turn result | | Find the last pair | All cards are matched; the final status and win banner are visible | A combined pair-found and completion sentence | | New Game or Restart | The replacement board is closed, with cleared moves and elapsed time | The previous turn text is cleared | The table describes normal play. An imported unfinished snapshot has an additional paused state, discussed below. The full selection rules belong in Turn resolution and Selection state. ## A closed card and a revealed card carry different information `Board.tsx` computes the visible positions through `faceUpCards` and passes a face number to `Card.tsx` only for those positions. Every other card receives `face={null}`. In that case the card contains a `.card-back` span, a small neutral diamond, rather than face artwork. The hidden face is also absent from the card's accessible name. Silence does not create a separate information path that reveals identities early. `describeCard` in `src/game/board/card-state.ts` produces the class state and label from the card's position, visible face and matched flag. The first hidden card on any board is named: > Row 1, column 1, closed For face 0, a revealed card at that position is named: > Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid circle, marker top After its pair is found, the same position is named: > Row 1, column 1, matched, cyan solid circle, marker top The inline SVG is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. The button name carries the semantic description instead of making the player traverse individual paths and circles. The check SVG is hidden from the accessibility tree in the same way; the button's matched state supplies its meaning. See Screen reader notes and Card artwork. ## Identity survives loss of color A revealed face uses shape, marker position and fill. Color reinforces the marker distinction. `faceDesign` in `src/game/board/face-design.ts` maps a face ID to those parts and to the phrase used in the button name. Faces 0 and 64 both have a cyan circle with a top marker, but one is solid and the other outlined. The drawing and name preserve that difference. See Pair identity for the full model. There is also a deliberate difference between a face's marker and a matched card's check. The marker belongs to identity and can appear in different directions. The check belongs to outcome and stays in the card's top-right corner. In `card.css` the check occupies 16% of the card's width and height. The nearby comment explains that a wider mark would reach the top-right identity marker. That is a concrete example of feedback being added around the memory task rather than covering the information the player is trying to retain. ## A match stays readable A match takes effect on the second eligible reveal. The pair goes into `game.matched`, selection returns to `closed`, and both cards remain face up. The player does not wait for a sound or for an animation to finish before the result exists. Matched cards use the Green border, `#8BEA7D`, and a check mark in the same color. They retain full opacity. The border helps with scanning; the check makes the matched condition visible without relying on the border's hue. Their faces remain available for orientation as the rest of the board changes. `Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` rather than using the native `disabled` attribute. A matched card remains reachable by board navigation and still has its position and face name. Its activation has no game effect. This matters when the player crosses a completed part of the board: focus movement remains spatially predictable, and an announced matched state explains why that card cannot start another pair. # React boundaries This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering. React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events. ## The mounted tree `src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions. The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation. These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory. ## The data-only side `deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React. The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree. This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. No such migration is implemented in the source. ## What remains unchanged in the implementation `PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer. The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. Preferences store and Storage failure policy describe the existing behavior. ## Alternatives and tradeoffs Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions. A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves. ## Reading the rule accurately The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended. The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries. This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data. ## The current preferences key and value shape These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences. # Shared-device competition This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs. Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game. ## Where the product stands Neon Pairs supports solo play and Tournament mode. `src/game/Game.tsx` keeps the solo session mounted while the separate `src/game/tournament/` feature owns tournament participants, bracket progression, exchange validation and history. Both modes reuse the same card board and game rules, while tournament completions stay outside solo preferences. The feature remains a local social activity, not a remote ranking service. The detailed pages identify bracket rules, deal identity, result comparison and saved-result boundaries; Tournament mode describes the player journey and JSON format. The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them. ## Why share a device A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file. Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur. Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature. ## Three things people are following An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position. These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks. The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. Pairing covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. Rounds covers event stages. Boards and deals distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. Ties and scores address results from different angles. ## A local social activity, with local evidence The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers. The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine. Reproducibility explains the existing technical tools. Competition research describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together. ## How the current code helps The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering. The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later. The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. Architecture, session module and React boundaries give the broader engineering context. # ADR 057: Split the view by behavior This record explains the component boundaries and the targeted rendering work that keeps large boards responsive. ## Context A single game component could contain the select, status, 256 buttons, snapshot editor, timers and storage effects. That would be quick to start and difficult to review once input, import and visibility interact. The project instead separates the view by behavior while keeping the composition easy to follow. `Game.tsx` is the assembly point. `Controls` owns deal actions, `GameStatus` renders progress and completion, `Board` renders and navigates cards, and `Reproduction` owns the disclosure and drafts. Browser session behavior lives behind `useGame`. These boundaries correspond to real responsibilities rather than a generic component taxonomy. ## Small does not mean responsibility-free `Card` is a leaf button with the state descriptor, face renderer and event callbacks it needs. `Board` calculates face-up and matched membership and supplies positional props. `useBoardFocus` owns remembered focus and navigation. The session controller decides how an activation changes the game and when browser time is synchronized. This arrangement prevents a card from reading storage or deciding whether a snapshot load should pause. It also prevents the controller from querying every button to paint its revealed state. Each layer can be understood in terms of the data or browser effect it actually owns. React boundaries explains those connections. ## A concrete rendering concern The active clock can update often, and a 16x16 board contains many buttons. The board memoizes the face-up set from matched positions and selection, and separately memoizes matched membership. It passes a stable activation callback that reads the latest handler through a ref. `Card` is memoized. A pure clock tick that preserves selection and matched arrays therefore does not force every unchanged card to render again. The optimization follows an observed repeating update. It is not a reason to make every value global or to hide the data flow behind a subscription framework. ## Styles and tests follow the boundary Card styles sit with `Card`, board layout with `Board`, status styles with `GameStatus`, and control styles with controls. The diagnostic face sheet renders the actual card outside the main controls to verify that its appearance does not depend on unrelated parent styling. That is useful evidence that the component owns its own presentation. Focused tests sit near the associated behavior, while browser journeys span the assembled application. The source-size specification aims for 100 lines per TypeScript file and limits authored files to 200 lines. The audit checks that ceiling. These constraints keep authored files reviewable. ## Alternatives

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.
