# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

Solo New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly. Tournament's Leave tournament action uses a native dialog before discarding an unfinished event.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

Tournament owns the current leave route. Its confirmation explains that unfinished progress will be discarded, focuses Keep playing when opened, and treats Escape as Keep playing. Focus policy covers orientation when the Tournament screen replaces the solo controls.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. Reproduction panel documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions
# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in Rules.

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in Reproducibility. A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in Board keyboard navigation.

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is Native controls guide for element choice, Focus policy for page orientation and New game and restart for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.

13:Tournament owns the current leave route. Its confirmation explains that unfinished progress will be discarded, focuses Keep playing when opened, and treats Escape as Keep playing. Focus policy covers orientation when the Tournament screen replaces the solo controls.
17:`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.
19:BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.
21:The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. Reproduction panel documents the actual disclosure.
23:This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.
27:The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.
31:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
33:No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. 37:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
39:The solo session has no confirmation surface and keeps its existing timing behavior. Tournament pauses its active turn clock while the Leave tournament confirmation is open, including a pending mismatch interval, and resumes with a fresh clock observation when the person keeps playing. Clock design and Mismatch interval explain the established clock model.
41:Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in competition deals.

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage        | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| ------------ | ----------- | ----- | ---------- |
| Quarterfinal | 4           | 16    | 8          |
| Semifinal    | 6           | 36    | 18         |
| Final        | 8           | 64    | 32         |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

Face catalogue, pair identity and card artwork cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See large board rendering, layout grid and zoom behaviour.

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. Board keyboard navigation covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The ordinary `Controls` component still renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. Tournament mode uses its own stage mapping: Quarterfinal 4x4, Semifinal 6x6 and Final 8x8. The technical size catalogue and event choice remain separate.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in competition pairing, and the dimensions of the playing board are in competition boards.

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. TournamentPlay renders its `Round:` and `Now playing:` context separately from those solo labels.

`src/game/Game.tsx` composes the solo session or Tournament screen. The solo path passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. The tournament path passes the active match into `TournamentPlay`, which owns the round context. `session.generation` remains a solo deal lifetime counter.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Reusing the solo status component does not supply a round label automatically; TournamentPlay renders event context separately from ordinary game statistics.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. Mismatch interval and new game and restart cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. Focus policy and dialog policy describe the existing interactions.
# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. Tournament mode stores participants and bracket results under `src/game/tournament/`; the card engine remains unaware of player identity. Choosing a board, recording a finished attempt and interpreting a tied result remain separate decisions.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| -------------- | ------- | ---- |
| First          | Ada     | 1    |
| Second         | Bo      | 2    |
| Third          | Cora    | 3    |
| Fourth         | Dev     | 4    |
| Fifth          | Emi     | 5    |
| Sixth          | Finn    | 6    |
| Seventh        | Gia     | 7    |
| Eighth         | Hal     | 8    |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

Competition deals covers board identity. Competition ties covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores.

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.
# Tournament mode

Tournament mode is a shared-device knockout event. It keeps participant, match and result data outside ordinary solo preferences while reusing the existing board rules and active clock.

## Set up and pair players

Choose 4 or 8 players. The screen provides fields labelled Player 1 through Player 8; only the chosen number is enabled. Names are trimmed, internal whitespace is collapsed, and text is normalized to NFC when accepted. Each name must have 2 to 20 Unicode code points. Names compare without regard to case within this tournament.

Entry order assigns seeds. Four players open as seed 1 versus 4, then 2 versus 3. Eight players open as 1 versus 8, 4 versus 5, 3 versus 6, then 2 versus 7. Winners advance along those pairings to the Semifinal and Final. A four-player bracket begins at the Semifinal.

Quarterfinals use 4x4 boards, Semifinals use 6x6 boards and Finals use 8x8 boards. Every match receives a unique full board code within the event. Both players in a match start fresh games from that same code, one after the other. The Start turn action begins each attempt; Next turn hands the same deal to the other player. Next match moves to the following bracket match after both results exist. Leave tournament asks for confirmation before discarding an unfinished event and pauses active time until the choice is made.

## Results and game boundary

Fewer moves wins a match. Equal move counts use lower active elapsed time; if those values are exactly equal, the lower seed wins. Elapsed comparisons use the in-memory millisecond values, including fractions. The bracket displays each player's moves and formatted time, with the match winner identified in its own column. At the end, the screen shows `Champion: NAME`.

Tournament games use the normal matching, mismatch and active-time rules. They never change the solo saved size or per-size best moves. Tournament play uses its own React state and clock adapter; it does not call the solo completion path.

## Tournament JSON

The Tournament JSON field accepts a versioned `neon-pairs/tournament` object. Export writes alphabetized keys and includes the bracket, deal codes, completed results and an in-progress game snapshot when there is one. Exporting a setup screen preserves the selected player count and name drafts. Loading validates the complete value before replacing the tournament or setup. Unknown fields show `Unknown field: NAME.`; other rejected values show `Invalid tournament.`. A loaded in-progress turn waits for Start turn before active time or card actions resume.

The export is copyable text. It uses no clipboard API or network service. Tournament JSON is separate from board codes, game snapshots and browser storage.

## Past tournaments and storage

Finished tournaments are added to Past tournaments and remain there after reload. The newest 10 records are retained. They use the feature envelope `{ "v": 3, "items": [...] }` at `np3:tournaments`; the existing preferences key stays unchanged. Past brackets can be viewed when no active event would be replaced. Active tournament progress remains in memory and is not saved to browser storage; Export puts JSON in the field for manual transfer. If browser storage is unavailable, the current event still works and the screen says `Progress won't be saved on this device.`

The browser has no account service or remote tournament results. Imported JSON is validated for plausible structure and game consistency, but it does not prove who played or certify a result.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The ordinary `Controls` component still renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. Tournament mode uses its own stage mapping: Quarterfinal 4x4, Semifinal 6x6 and Final 8x8. The technical size catalogue and event choice remain separate.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in competition pairing, and the dimensions of the playing board are in competition boards.

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. TournamentPlay renders its `Round:` and `Now playing:` context separately from those solo labels.

`src/game/Game.tsx` composes the solo session or Tournament screen. The solo path passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. The tournament path passes the active match into `TournamentPlay`, which owns the round context. `session.generation` remains a solo deal lifetime counter.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Reusing the solo status component does not supply a round label automatically; TournamentPlay renders event context separately from ordinary game statistics.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. Mismatch interval and new game and restart cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. Focus policy and dialog policy describe the existing interactions.
# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. Tournament mode stores participants and bracket results under `src/game/tournament/`; the card engine remains unaware of player identity. Choosing a board, recording a finished attempt and interpreting a tied result remain separate decisions.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| -------------- | ------- | ---- |
| First          | Ada     | 1    |
| Second         | Bo      | 2    |
| Third          | Cora    | 3    |
| Fourth         | Dev     | 4    |
| Fifth          | Emi     | 5    |
| Sixth          | Finn    | 6    |
| Seventh        | Gia     | 7    |
| Eighth         | Hal     | 8    |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

Competition deals covers board identity. Competition ties covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores.

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.
# Tournament mode

Tournament mode is a shared-device knockout event. It keeps participant, match and result data outside ordinary solo preferences while reusing the existing board rules and active clock.

## Set up and pair players

Choose 4 or 8 players. The screen provides fields labelled Player 1 through Player 8; only the chosen number is enabled. Names are trimmed, internal whitespace is collapsed, and text is normalized to NFC when accepted. Each name must have 2 to 20 Unicode code points. Names compare without regard to case within this tournament.

Entry order assigns seeds. Four players open as seed 1 versus 4, then 2 versus 3. Eight players open as 1 versus 8, 4 versus 5, 3 versus 6, then 2 versus 7. Winners advance along those pairings to the Semifinal and Final. A four-player bracket begins at the Semifinal.

Quarterfinals use 4x4 boards, Semifinals use 6x6 boards and Finals use 8x8 boards. Every match receives a unique full board code within the event. Both players in a match start fresh games from that same code, one after the other. The Start turn action begins each attempt; Next turn hands the same deal to the other player. Next match moves to the following bracket match after both results exist. Leave tournament asks for confirmation before discarding an unfinished event and pauses active time until the choice is made.

## Results and game boundary

Fewer moves wins a match. Equal move counts use lower active elapsed time; if those values are exactly equal, the lower seed wins. Elapsed comparisons use the in-memory millisecond values, including fractions. The bracket displays each player's moves and formatted time, with the match winner identified in its own column. At the end, the screen shows `Champion: NAME`.

Tournament games use the normal matching, mismatch and active-time rules. They never change the solo saved size or per-size best moves. Tournament play uses its own React state and clock adapter; it does not call the solo completion path.

## Tournament JSON

The Tournament JSON field accepts a versioned `neon-pairs/tournament` object. Export writes alphabetized keys and includes the bracket, deal codes, completed results and an in-progress game snapshot when there is one. Exporting a setup screen preserves the selected player count and name drafts. Loading validates the complete value before replacing the tournament or setup. Unknown fields show `Unknown field: NAME.`; other rejected values show `Invalid tournament.`. A loaded in-progress turn waits for Start turn before active time or card actions resume.

The export is copyable text. It uses no clipboard API or network service. Tournament JSON is separate from board codes, game snapshots and browser storage.

## Past tournaments and storage

Finished tournaments are added to Past tournaments and remain there after reload. The newest 10 records are retained. They use the feature envelope `{ "v": 3, "items": [...] }` at `np3:tournaments`; the existing preferences key stays unchanged. Past brackets can be viewed when no active event would be replaced. Active tournament progress remains in memory and is not saved to browser storage; Export puts JSON in the field for manual transfer. If browser storage is unavailable, the current event still works and the screen says `Progress won't be saved on this device.`

The browser has no account service or remote tournament results. Imported JSON is validated for plausible structure and game consistency, but it does not prove who played or certify a result.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. When using request_user_input_async, you can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. # Tournament mode

Tournament mode is a shared-device knockout event. It keeps participant, match and result data outside ordinary solo preferences while reusing the existing board rules and active clock.

## Set up and pair players

Choose 4 or 8 players. The screen provides fields labelled Player 1 through Player 8; only the chosen number is enabled. Names are trimmed, internal whitespace is collapsed, and text is normalized to NFC when accepted. Each name must have 2 to 20 Unicode code points. Names compare without regard to case within this tournament.

Entry order assigns seeds. Four players open as seed 1 versus 4, then 2 versus 3. Eight players open as 1 versus 8, 4 versus 5, 3 versus 6, then 2 versus 7. Winners advance along those pairings to the Semifinal and Final. A four-player bracket begins at the Semifinal.

Quarterfinals use 4x4 boards, Semifinals use 6x6 boards and Finals use 8x8 boards. Every match receives a unique full board code within the event. Both players in a match start fresh games from that same code, one after the other. The Start turn action begins each attempt; Next turn hands the same deal to the other player. Next match moves to the following bracket match after both results exist. Leave tournament asks for confirmation before discarding an unfinished event and pauses active time until the choice is made.

The shared status shows `Round: NAME` and `Now playing: NAME` during a turn. Once a game ends it identifies who is next; after both results it identifies the match winner. The champion appears at the end.

## Results and game boundary

Fewer moves wins a match. Equal move counts use lower active elapsed time; if those values are exactly equal, the lower seed wins. Elapsed comparisons use the in-memory millisecond values, including fractions. The bracket displays each player's moves and formatted time, with the match winner identified in its own column. At the end, the screen shows `Champion: NAME`.

Tournament games use the normal matching, mismatch and active-time rules. They never change the solo saved size or per-size best moves. Tournament play uses its own React state and clock adapter; it does not call the solo completion path.

## Tournament JSON

The Tournament JSON field accepts a versioned `neon-pairs/tournament` object. Export writes alphabetized keys and includes the bracket, deal codes, completed results and an in-progress game snapshot when there is one. Exporting a setup screen preserves the selected player count and name drafts. Loading validates the complete value before replacing the tournament or setup. A valid load that would replace an active event asks for confirmation first. Unknown fields show `Unknown field: NAME.`; other rejected values show `Invalid tournament.`. A loaded in-progress turn waits for Start turn before active time or card actions resume.

The export is copyable text. It uses no clipboard API or network service. Tournament JSON is separate from board codes, game snapshots and browser storage.

## Past tournaments and storage

Finished tournaments are added to Past tournaments with their players, champion and match count, and remain there after reload. The newest 10 records are retained. They use the feature envelope `{ "v": 3, "items": [...] }` at `np3:tournaments`; the existing preferences key stays unchanged. Active tournament progress remains in memory and is not saved to browser storage; Export puts JSON in the field for manual transfer. If browser storage is unavailable, the current event still works and the screen says `Progress won't be saved on this device.`

The browser has no account service or remote tournament results. Imported JSON is validated for plausible structure and game consistency, but it does not prove who played or certify a result.
# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. Tournament comparison lives outside the single-game transitions in `src/game/tournament/rules.ts`.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| ----------- | ----- | --------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Ada         | 12    | 70200                       | Ahead on moves         |
| Bo          | 13    | 58100                       | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example          |
| ----------- | ----- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Cora        | 15    | 65200                       | Ahead on active time            |
| Dev         | 15    | 65900                       | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. Competition pairing supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The single-game core has no opponent or entrant data; the Tournament rules supply seed comparison separately.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

Elapsed time rules, clock design and mismatch interval describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those are single-game rules; the tournament comparator applies their completed move and active-time values in the order defined above.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.
# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in competition deals.

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage        | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| ------------ | ----------- | ----- | ---------- |
| Quarterfinal | 4           | 16    | 8          |
| Semifinal    | 6           | 36    | 18         |
| Final        | 8           | 64    | 32         |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

Face catalogue, pair identity and card artwork cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See large board rendering, layout grid and zoom behaviour.

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. Board keyboard navigation covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The ordinary `Controls` component still renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. Tournament mode uses its own stage mapping: Quarterfinal 4x4, Semifinal 6x6 and Final 8x8. The technical size catalogue and event choice remain separate.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
